Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN) -- The designers behind a "thinking" yacht are hoping to break a world record by sending it across the Atlantic Ocean without any human assistance. The autonomous yacht Avalon is hoisted to have her keel put in place before launching . The four-meter boat, "Avalon", was designed and built by an eight-strong team of third-year engineering students at Swiss science university ETH Zurich. The students are planning to take the boat to a robotic sailing regatta in July, before launching it into the Microtransat Transatlantic challenge in early September. Using sensors to detect the speed and direction of the wind, the boat is programmed to reach a given co-ordinate and will attain it by automatically adapting to the changing conditions. One of the "Students Sailing Autonomously" (SSA) team's project managers, Hendrik Erckens, told CNN that if the Atlantic crossing succeeds it will be a world record as an unmanned boat has not previously made the voyage. It is planned the crossing will begin from the west coast of Ireland and finish in the Caribbean. "For us the Microtransat challenge is the big goal. I'm pretty confident we can do it. This week in testing it is pretty much doing what it's supposed to do. And it is water tight. "Over the last couple of days we tried some autonomous tacks and jibes and now we are testing the navigation," he said. See photos of the autonomous yacht from construction to launch » . The team has been working on the project since September 2008, and are currently at the on-water testing stage, having designed and built the boat. While the team will be able to track the boat through an onboard global positioning system (GPS) during the transatlantic voyage, Erckens said as long as the challenge is active they won't have any control over the vessel. "We will set it out and it will be completely autonomous. There are solar cells on the back for power and extra power supplies on board. "There is a satellite communication system on board and the boat can download weather information by itself so it can calculate the best route to travel," he said. Erckens said the team is positive that the carbon-fibre boat will survive the rough Atlantic seas -- an issue that has stopped many manned crossings before -- including Richard Branson's attempt at the fastest transatlantic crossing aboard the 99-foot Virgin Money last fall. "We feel our advantage over other teams is that we are mechanical engineers. We have designed this boat ourselves and exactly for this purpose." Erckens said the idea could one day offer a new autopilot option for large yachts. "The idea came as there are autopilots for boats out there, but currently the commercially available autopilots only steer the rudder. We are looking to control the sails as well."

LONDON, England (CNN) — The creators of a “thinking” yacht hope to set a world record by guiding it across the Atlantic with no human involvement.

The autonomous yacht, named **Avalon**, is a four-meter vessel designed and constructed by a team of eight third-year engineering students at **ETH Zurich**, Switzerland’s science university. Before being launched, the boat was lifted so that its keel could be installed.

The students plan to enter Avalon in a robotic sailing regatta in July, then send it into the **Microtransat Transatlantic Challenge** in early September. The yacht uses sensors to measure wind speed and direction, and it is programmed to travel to a specific set of coordinates by adjusting itself automatically as conditions change.

Hendrik Erckens, one of the project managers for the **Students Sailing Autonomously** team, told CNN that a successful Atlantic crossing would establish a world record, because no unmanned boat has ever completed the journey before. The planned route would start on Ireland’s west coast and end in the Caribbean.

“For us, the Microtransat challenge is the major objective. I’m quite confident that we can manage it. During testing this week, it has mostly been doing what it is meant to do. And it is watertight,” Erckens said.

“In the past few days, we have tested some autonomous tacks and jibes, and now we are working on the navigation,” he added.

The group has been developing the project since September 2008. After designing and building the vessel, they are now carrying out tests on the water.

During the transatlantic attempt, the team will be able to monitor Avalon through an onboard **GPS** system. However, Erckens said that once the challenge is underway, they will not be allowed to control the boat in any way.

“We will launch it, and from that point it will operate entirely on its own. It has solar panels at the back to provide power, along with additional power supplies on board,” he said.

“There is also a satellite communication system, and the boat can retrieve weather data by itself so that it can work out the most suitable route,” Erckens explained.

He said the team believes the carbon-fiber yacht can withstand the difficult conditions of the Atlantic, which have caused problems for many crewed crossings in the past. One example was Richard Branson’s attempt the previous autumn to make the fastest transatlantic crossing in the 99-foot **Virgin Money**.

Erckens said the students think their strength lies in their engineering background.

“We believe our advantage over other teams is that we are mechanical engineers. We designed this boat ourselves specifically for this mission,” he said.

He also suggested that the technology could eventually lead to a new kind of autopilot system for larger yachts.

“The idea came from the fact that autopilots for boats already exist, but the commercially available versions currently only control the rudder. We want to control the sails as well,” Erckens said.

**ETH Zurich students set sail for transatlantic robotics milestone with autonomous yacht Avalon**

*Zurich, Switzerland* — A team of engineering students from ETH Zurich is preparing to send an autonomous yacht named **Avalon** into one of the most demanding proving grounds in robotics: the open Atlantic Ocean.

Their goal is to compete in the **Microtransat Challenge**, an international contest that asks small, unmanned sailing vessels to cross the Atlantic without human control. If successful, Avalon would join a short list of robotic craft capable of navigating thousands of kilometers through shifting winds, waves, currents and weather — all while making its own decisions at sea.

Avalon is not a radio-controlled boat. Once underway, the yacht is designed to sail independently, using onboard sensors, GPS navigation, wind instruments and a computer control system to plot a course and adjust its sails and rudder. The vessel must manage the same basic tasks as a human sailor: determine wind direction, choose efficient headings, avoid dangerous conditions and conserve energy.

For the ETH Zurich team, the project is both a technical challenge and an engineering education in miniature ocean-going autonomy. Unlike autonomous cars or drones, a robotic sailboat cannot simply rely on constant engine power. It must harvest energy from the environment, use wind for propulsion and ensure its electronics remain powered during a journey that could last weeks or longer.

The Microtransat Challenge has long attracted universities, hobbyists and research groups interested in marine robotics. The rules are simple in concept but difficult in execution: build a small autonomous sailing boat and get it across the Atlantic. In practice, the challenge is punishing. Saltwater corrosion, storms, software failures, battery limitations and mechanical stress can end a voyage long before the finish line.

Avalon’s designers have focused on durability and redundancy, recognizing that any failure at sea may be impossible to fix. The yacht must withstand long periods without maintenance while continuing to make navigational decisions in an unpredictable environment.

Autonomous sailing vessels are of growing interest beyond competition. Researchers see potential uses in climate monitoring, oceanographic data collection, marine surveillance and long-duration environmental missions. Because sailboats can travel using wind power, they offer the possibility of extended operations with relatively low energy demands.

But first, Avalon must prove it can survive the Atlantic.

For the students behind the project, the journey represents more than a race. It is a test of whether a small, student-built machine can combine mechanical engineering, software, electronics and naval design into a vessel capable of crossing an ocean on its own.

If Avalon succeeds, it would mark a significant achievement for ETH Zurich’s young engineers — and another step toward a future in which autonomous vessels routinely explore the world’s oceans without a crew on board.

**Swiss Students Build Four-Meter Unmanned Sailboat to Attempt Autonomous Atlantic Crossing**

*Lausanne, Switzerland* — A team of Swiss students has designed and built a four-meter unmanned sailing boat intended to cross the Atlantic Ocean without any human control, in an ambitious test of autonomous navigation, renewable energy systems and small-craft ocean engineering.

The vessel, developed as a student-led engineering project, is designed to sail entirely on its own, using onboard computers, sensors and automated sail controls to navigate changing weather, waves and shipping traffic. If successful, the craft would demonstrate that a small, wind-powered autonomous boat can survive one of the world’s most demanding ocean passages while operating independently for weeks or even months.

The boat is roughly the size of a small dinghy, but its mission is far more complex. Unlike a remote-controlled craft, it is not meant to be steered continuously from shore. Instead, it must make decisions on its own: plotting a course, trimming its sails, managing its power supply, avoiding dangerous conditions and maintaining communication with the team whenever possible.

### A Student Project With Ocean-Going Ambitions

The project brings together students from several technical disciplines, including mechanical engineering, robotics, electronics, computer science and naval architecture. Their goal is to create a robust autonomous sailing platform capable of completing a transatlantic journey with no crew onboard and no direct human steering.

The boat’s small size presents one of the biggest engineering challenges. A four-meter hull has limited space for batteries, solar panels, control electronics, communications equipment and mechanical systems. Every component must be light, durable and energy-efficient, while also capable of withstanding saltwater, strong winds, heavy waves and long periods without maintenance.

The students have focused on reliability rather than speed. The vessel does not need to break records; it needs to keep moving, protect its systems and survive. Its design prioritizes stability, low power consumption and fail-safe operation.

### How the Boat Sails Itself

The autonomous sailing boat uses a combination of onboard sensors and navigation software to determine its position and adjust its course. A GPS receiver provides location data, while a compass, wind sensors and motion sensors help the boat understand its orientation, speed and sailing conditions.

Using this information, the onboard computer calculates how to steer and how to set the sail. Small electric actuators control the rudder and sail system. The software must account for the fact that a sailboat cannot sail directly into the wind; it must tack back and forth at angles, choosing routes that balance progress, wind direction and safety.

The boat is expected to use solar panels to recharge its batteries, allowing it to operate for extended periods without fuel. Energy management is critical: communications, computing, steering and sail adjustment all consume power, and poor weather can reduce solar charging.

Satellite communication equipment would allow the team to receive status updates and track the boat’s position, though the vessel is designed to continue operating even if communications are temporarily lost.

### Crossing the Atlantic Without a Crew

A transatlantic crossing is a severe test for any vessel, especially one with no human aboard. The boat must endure storms, large swells, strong currents, shifting winds and possible collisions with floating debris. It must also comply with maritime safety expectations, including visibility and tracking, so other vessels can identify or avoid it.

Autonomous boats face a particularly difficult challenge in collision avoidance. Large commercial ships can be detected through maritime tracking systems such as AIS, but smaller boats, fishing gear, buoys or debris may be harder to identify. The students’ vessel must therefore combine conservative routing with onboard decision-making designed to reduce risk.

The exact launch route and timing depend heavily on seasonal weather patterns, testing progress and safety approvals. Student teams attempting such missions often choose routes that take advantage of prevailing winds and currents, while avoiding the most dangerous storm seasons.

### A Platform for Future Ocean Research

Beyond the symbolic goal of crossing the Atlantic, the project could have practical applications. Autonomous sailing boats are increasingly seen as useful tools for ocean monitoring, climate research, pollution tracking and marine data collection. Unlike powered drones or crewed vessels, wind-driven autonomous boats can travel long distances with minimal energy use and relatively low operating costs.

A successful voyage would show that small, inexpensive robotic sailing craft can collect data across remote ocean regions where research ships are costly to operate. Such vessels could one day monitor water temperature, salinity, currents, marine life or microplastic pollution over long periods.

For the students, the project is also a real-world engineering test. Designing an autonomous ocean-going sailboat requires more than laboratory simulations. Every component must work under conditions that are wet, unstable, corrosive and unpredictable.

### High Risk, High Learning Value

The team acknowledges that the mission is risky. Many autonomous ocean-crossing attempts have failed because of storms, equipment failures, power problems or loss of communication. A small boat at sea is exposed to forces far beyond what it experiences during lake or coastal trials.

But even if the boat does not complete the crossing, the project is expected to provide valuable data. Each test run helps the students improve the vessel’s hardware, software and decision-making systems. Failures can reveal weak points in waterproofing, mechanics, energy storage or navigation logic.

The students’ work reflects a broader trend in marine robotics: using compact, renewable-energy vessels to explore and monitor the oceans with minimal human intervention. Their four-meter sailboat may be small, but its mission points toward a future in which autonomous craft play a larger role in maritime science, navigation and environmental protection.

If the Swiss-built vessel succeeds in crossing the Atlantic without human control, it would mark a significant achievement for student engineering and a notable step forward in autonomous sailing technology.

**LONDON (CNN) —** In a marina workshop thousands of miles from the open ocean, a team of engineers is preparing a yacht designed to sail without a crew, relying instead on GPS, satellite navigation and renewable power to find its way across the water.

The autonomous yacht, **Avalon**, is being developed as a testbed for long-distance unmanned sailing — a vessel capable of plotting its position, adjusting course and managing energy without human hands on the helm.

Project manager **Hendrik Erckens** said the goal is to prove that an ocean-going yacht can operate safely and efficiently using a combination of onboard sensors and remote oversight.

> “Avalon is not just a boat with a computer attached,” Erckens said. “It is a complete autonomous system that has to understand where it is, where it is going and how to preserve enough energy to keep sailing.”

At the heart of the yacht’s navigation system is **GPS**, which continuously provides Avalon with its position at sea. That information is combined with digital charts and onboard control software to determine the yacht’s route and adjust its heading. If wind, current or waves push the vessel off course, the system can calculate corrections and steer the boat back toward its planned track.

Avalon also uses **satellite navigation and communications** to support long-range operation beyond the reach of coastal radio or cellular networks. Satellite links allow the team to monitor the yacht’s status, receive location updates and send revised mission instructions if conditions change.

> “Once the yacht is offshore, you cannot depend on ordinary communications,” Erckens said. “Satellite navigation gives us the global reach we need, and satellite communications allow us to keep an eye on the vessel wherever it is.”

Power is another central challenge. Unlike conventional yachts, Avalon is designed to operate for extended periods without refueling. **Solar panels** mounted on the vessel help recharge its batteries, supplying electricity for navigation computers, steering systems, communications equipment and sensors.

The team says solar power is essential for endurance. While the yacht uses the wind for propulsion, its autonomous systems still need a reliable electrical supply.

> “The wind moves the boat, but the electronics make autonomy possible,” Erckens said. “Solar power is what allows Avalon to keep thinking, communicating and navigating for long periods at sea.”

Autonomous vessels such as Avalon could eventually be used for marine research, environmental monitoring and long-duration ocean observation, reducing the need to send crews into remote or dangerous waters. But the project also faces major hurdles, including collision avoidance, harsh weather, mechanical reliability and compliance with maritime rules designed around human-operated ships.

Erckens said those challenges are exactly why the project matters.

> “The ocean is a demanding environment,” he said. “If Avalon can operate there, it shows what autonomous marine technology may be capable of in the future.”

For now, the yacht remains both an engineering experiment and a glimpse of a possible future in which vessels cross oceans guided by satellites, powered by the sun and steered by software.

**“Thinking” Yacht Readies for Robotic Regatta Before Atlantic Test**

On a grey morning beside an Irish marina, a small yacht nosed into the wind, hesitated, and then trimmed its sail without a hand on the sheet. There was no skipper aboard, no crew calling tactics, no one leaning over the rail. Instead, a cluster of sensors, onboard computers and software made the decisions: where to steer, when to tack, how to conserve power and how to stay upright when the weather turns foul.

Its builders call it a “thinking” yacht — not because it is conscious, but because it can make sailing decisions on its own.

The experimental vessel is being put through its final trials ahead of a robotic sailing regatta, where autonomous boats will compete to navigate courses using only wind, electronics and code. If those tests go well, the yacht’s next challenge will be far more ambitious: the Microtransat, an attempt to cross the Atlantic from Ireland to the Caribbean without human intervention.

For roboticists, sailors and ocean engineers, the project sits at the edge of several disciplines. The craft must behave like a sailor, a weather station and a survival machine all at once. It has to read the wind, sense its position, avoid dangerous manoeuvres, manage its limited electrical supply and keep moving for weeks through one of the world’s most unpredictable environments.

During trials, the boat’s masthead instruments measure wind speed and direction while GPS fixes its position. A digital compass and motion sensors track heading, heel and pitch. The onboard computer processes the information and sends commands to electric actuators controlling the rudder and sails. Solar panels help keep the system alive, feeding batteries that must last through cloud, salt spray and long nights at sea.

The robotic regatta will provide a controlled but revealing test. On a marked course, the yacht will need to round buoys, hold a course and respond to shifting winds faster than a human support team can intervene. Engineers will be watching for the small failures that can become large ones offshore: a sluggish tack, a confused sensor reading, an overcorrection in gusty conditions.

But the Microtransat is the real proving ground. The event has long been regarded as one of the toughest benchmarks in autonomous marine navigation. Unlike remote-controlled boats, Microtransat entries must sail independently. Once launched, they are expected to make their own decisions across thousands of miles of open ocean.

The route from Ireland to the Caribbean offers a punishing examination. The yacht must first escape coastal waters, where tides, traffic and confused seas complicate navigation. Then comes the open Atlantic, with fast-moving weather systems, steep waves and the constant risk of mechanical fatigue. Later, as it moves south and west, lighter winds and tropical conditions bring different hazards: heat, calms, squalls and the possibility of hurricane-season disturbances.

A successful crossing would not simply be a sporting achievement. Autonomous sailing craft could one day be used for oceanographic research, climate monitoring, fisheries protection and long-duration surveillance in remote waters. Wind-powered robots offer one major advantage over many powered drones: they can potentially remain at sea for months, using sails for propulsion and solar energy for electronics.

Still, the ocean is an unforgiving laboratory. Salt corrodes contacts. Ropes chafe. Sensors drift. A single line jammed at the wrong moment can end a mission. The challenge for the team is not only to teach the yacht to sail, but to teach it to cope when sailing stops going to plan.

For now, the little boat continues its rehearsals — tacking, correcting, learning through code refined after every outing. To spectators, it may look like a toy yacht with a technological twist. To its designers, it is a glimpse of a future in which vessels cross oceans with no one aboard, quietly collecting data, testing ideas and proving that seamanship can be translated, at least in part, into software.

If it reaches the Caribbean, the achievement will belong as much to the programmers as to the boatbuilders. But out on the Atlantic, with no hands on the helm, the final decisions will be made by the yacht itself.
